title: Construct the Minimum Bitwise Array II
statement: Every entry of `nums` is a prime number. Build and return an array `ans` of the same length where, for each index `i`, `ans[i]` is the smallest non-negative integer satisfying `(ans[i] | (ans[i] + 1)) == nums[i]` (with `|` the bitwise OR). When no integer satisfies this for some `nums[i]`, put `-1` at that index instead.
notes:
## Intuition

Adding 1 to any `a` turns its trailing ones into zeros and its lowest 0 bit into a 1, so `a | (a + 1)` is just `a` with its lowest 0 bit switched on. Two facts follow. The result is always odd, so the only even prime, 2, has no answer. And for an odd `num`, a valid `a` is `num` with one bit of its trailing run of ones cleared: the ones below that bit survive in `a`, so the cleared bit is exactly the lowest zero that `a | (a + 1)` switches back on. Clearing the highest bit of that run removes the most value, giving the minimum. Scanning every `a` below `num` would also work, but `num` can be 10^9.

## Approach

1. Walk through `nums`, appending one answer per `num` to `ans`.
2. If `num` is even (only 2 can be), append `-1`.
3. Otherwise compute `lowestZero = (num + 1) & ~num`: the carry from adding 1 stops at the lowest 0 bit, and masking with `~num` keeps only that bit.
4. `lowestZero >> 1` is the top bit of the trailing ones; append `num ^ (lowestZero >> 1)`, which clears it.
5. Return `ans`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 3, 5, 7]`.

- `2` is even, so `-1`.
- `3 = 11`: `lowestZero = 100` (4), the bit below it is 2, and `3 ^ 2 = 1`. Check: `1 | 2 = 3`.
- `5 = 101`: `lowestZero = 010` (2), the bit below it is 1, and `5 ^ 1 = 4`. Check: `4 | 5 = 5`.
- `7 = 111`: `lowestZero = 1000` (8), the bit below it is 4, and `7 ^ 4 = 3`. Check: `3 | 4 = 7`.

The answer is `[-1, 1, 4, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): a constant number of bit operations per value.
- Space: O(1) besides the returned array.

## Pitfalls

- `num - 1` always satisfies the equation for odd `num`, but it is the minimum only when `num` ends in `01`; for 7 the answer is 3, not 6.
- Clear the top bit of the trailing ones, not the lowest set bit and not the lowest zero itself.
- `~num` is negative in JavaScript, yet `(num + 1) & ~num` still isolates one positive bit because values stay below 2^31.
- Do not test for primality or other evens: 2 is the only even input and the only `-1`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ans` | the answers built so far, one per value |
| `num` | the prime currently being solved |
| `lowestZero` | the lowest 0 bit of `num`, as a power of two |

narration.3: Solve each prime on its own.
narration.4: a | (a + 1) is always odd, so an even target, which can only be 2, has no answer.
narration.7: Adding 1 carries up to the lowest 0 bit of num; masking with ~num keeps just that bit.
narration.8: The bit just below it is the top of the trailing ones; clearing it gives the smallest valid value.
narration.11: Every prime has its smallest answer, so return the array.
